cells.tense: You are here with the question and the question is working.
cells.ask: Bring one real question to someone this week — not rhetorical — and let their answer stand without improving it.
cells.core:
You are good at this. Not just the asking — the itch to know. When something comes up, you turn it over. You pick it up, look at it from underneath, set it down carefully. People around you can feel that you actually want to understand, not just be seen understanding.

That is not a small thing. Most people ask to confirm. You ask to find out. The pull toward what is worth your attention is real, and you steer by it. What keeps this from settling into a shelf is that the pull stays alive when it has somewhere to go. So bring one question you actually hold into someone's hands this week. Let their answer be something you receive, not something you process.

cells.tense: You will have understood the whole thing before anyone has finished saying it.
cells.ask: Finish one conversation without reaching for the next level — ask one more question about what they said, and stop there.
cells.core:
You are ahead of the moment. The question is barely out and you already have three branches of where it could go, whose work it connects to, what it implies. That is real. It is also why you are not quite in the room.

Your understanding is running faster than the thing being understood. What gets missed is not the insight — it is the arrival. The slow part where a thing settles in you before it becomes material you can build with. You are reaching past the answer toward the next question before the first one has landed.

Let one exchange go unfinished this week. Ask about what they just said, and when the answer comes, let it be enough. See whether what you were chasing shows up on its own.

cells.tense: The asking happened once and the room you asked it in is already behind you.
cells.ask: Write one unfinished question somewhere you will see it tomorrow — no plan for answering it, just the question, in your own handwriting.
cells.core:
Curiosity is still in you. You can feel it when something catches — a brief lift, a leaning in — and then it goes quiet. As if the asking got answered once and the answer was not good, so the whole motion learned to stop before it starts.

It is not that you have nothing worth asking. It is that the question does not make it up and out anymore. The pull is still where it was. It is the looking up that stopped.

You do not have to point yourself at what it meant back then. Just put a question back where you can see it. Not to solve anything. So the motion has somewhere to go when it wakes up.

cells.tense: Your hand is already on the question, and you are calling it being attentive.
cells.ask: Tell one person about a question you are currently sitting with — not a solved one — and what you are noticing about it.
cells.core:
You probably describe yourself as thoughtful. Someone who listens, who asks good questions, who wants to understand where someone is coming from. That is real. It is also the shape your curiosity takes after it has been trained to serve.

You are asking the question that keeps the room open, not the question you actually hold. Your curiosity is doing its work — it is what makes you good at this — but you are handing it to the room before you have claimed it. The question is yours. You give it away before you have it.

Nothing is wrong here. But something is missing: the version of the question that is about what you want to know. Try saying it out loud in your own voice, to someone who can hold it.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that this person's curiosity is 'balanced' — the record shows a Seed-stage Initiate still forming, which is a beginning, not an achieved equilibrium. A reader could reasonably say 'I'm not sure I've arrived anywhere yet' and be right. The ask survives being wrong because offering one question into another's hands is a transferrable act of attention regardless of whether the diagnosis holds. The sentence that serves me more than them is anything that sounds like I'm praising an origin story I invented for their curiosity — 'you've always been this way' — which the record does not support.
